opus_only: The maturity-specific curve may be the sum of several components, each reverting at its own rate (eq. 4).

Habitat demand shifts spill to neighbouring maturities (close substitutes), so the maturity-specific deviation is a smooth curve averaging zero that is assumed to decay exponentially, which also meets the HJM no-arbitrage requirement.
M1 is humped with peak at tau = ln2/Km and a fixed shape scaled by the Ito process m(t).
Forecasts are judged by RMSE of predicted futures-implied forward rates and by profits of a simple trading strategy.
Footnote 6: NW statistic = mean of daily RMSE differences divided by its Newey-West standard error; Diebold-Mariano would be an alternative.
The training sample (1981-91) had forward rates near 9% and contracts only to about 4 years, versus about 6.2% and up to 10 years in the full sample.
Only Km (decay rate) and sigma*^2 (measurement-error variance) are optimised by QML; C0, C1, C2 come from the unconditional-curve fit.
Measurement equation: z_t = f(tau;t) - U_hat(tau) = A x_t + eps_t with row A_j = [e(tau_j)'M, e(tau_j)'D].
Footnote 8: state variables that would make diffusions negative are reset to the boundary value.
sonnet_only: M reflects preferred-habitat supply/demand at specific maturities; D reflects changing expectations of future spot rates.
The model class is arbitrage-free (HJM-verified), unlike simple curve-fitting forecasts.
Test target: forecast 90-day forward rates at future dates using a representative member of the model class.
Habitat effects stay local to a maturity region, they do not roll down toward spot, so they decay rather than shift.
Date-specific deviation derives from the Expectations Hypothesis (Fisher).
D(inf;t)=0, and D(0;t)=spot rate minus unconditional spot rate.
M arises from abnormal pricing at certain maturities driven by habitat and preferences of individual and institutional investors.
Close substitutability across nearby maturities justifies modelling M as a smooth curve.
No information on M dynamics, so exponential decay to zero is chosen as the simplest assumption (also needed for HJM no-arbitrage).
NW comparison vs buy-and-hold uses only days where signals differ; positive NW means CFRS better.
QML estimation: assume Gaussian innovations, optimise Km and sigma*^2 over the quasi-log-likelihood.

Kalman prediction and update equations (Eq 28-33): x_{t|t-1}=W x_{t-1|t-1}; P_{t|t-1}=W P W'+Q_t; update with gain P A' H^-1 v_t; H_t=A P A' + sigma*^2 I; ln L = -(nT/2) ln 2pi - 1/2 sum(ln|H_t| + v_t' H_t^-1 v_t).
Footnote 8: diffusion terms depend on the m states and must be non-negative, so states breaching the bound are reset to the nearest feasible value.
